title: Does going first win the bargain?
hook: You make the first offer on a shrinking pie, with no deadline. How much can you keep?

knows: backward induction: in a one-shot take-it-or-leave-it offer the proposer can keep almost everything (lowball-offer-should-pass)
money later is worth less than money now
doesNotKnow: that when each delay shrinks the pie, the first proposer gets 1/(1 + δ), a small edge when delays are cheap

misconception: Whoever makes the first offer can grab most of the pie.
objective: The learner can explain, by stepping back from a deadline, that the responder's power is the value of proposing next round, so with a 10% shrink the first proposer keeps 1/(1 + 0.9) ≈ 52.6%, and that a costlier delay (50% shrink) raises the first proposer's share to 2/3.

claims.text: With one round, the proposer keeps 100%: the other can only accept or get nothing.
claims.source: Backward induction in the one-round (ultimatum) game, with the responder accepting when indifferent; the convention used in lowball-offer-should-pass. Demo.tsx share(…, 1) = 1.

claims.text: Each added round in front, the proposer must offer the responder 90% of what the responder would keep as next round's proposer, and keeps the rest (for example 0.9 × 10.0% = 9.0% offered, 91.0% kept with three rounds).
claims.source: share(n) = 1 − δ · share(n − 1), δ = 0.9: 1, 0.1, 0.91, 0.181, … Demo.tsx share(). Builder re-run in node.

claims.text: With a 10% shrink per round, long games settle at 1 ÷ (1 + 0.9) = 52.6% for the first proposer; 400 rounds give 52.6%.
claims.source: share(n) = (1 − (−δ)^n) / (1 + δ). Node: 50 rounds 0.5236, 51 rounds 0.5288, 400 rounds 0.5263; 1/1.9 = 0.5263. Matches the brief's check (company/domains/briefs/economics.markets.md #24).

claims.text: With a 50% shrink the first proposer's share is 66.7%; the costlier the delay, the more going first is worth (30% shrink gives 58.8%).
This is a simplified model (Rubinstein's alternating offers): both players are rational and know the shrink rate.
claims.source: Rubinstein (1982), 'Perfect equilibrium in a bargaining model', Econometrica 50(1); Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 12 (advanced section). The model name is in this claim and the code, the learner sees 'a simplified model'. Fact-checker confirms.

recall.question: Two sides alternate offers with no deadline. Every rejected round, the money on the table shrinks a little (say 2%). Roughly how much does the side that offers first keep?
recall.why: The other side can wait one round and become the proposer, which is worth almost as much, so the first offer must give nearly half away: 1 ÷ (1 + 0.98) ≈ 50.5%.
